newsitem.title: FRANCE: French journalists strike over tax plan.
newsitem.headline: French journalists strike over tax plan.

text.p: French public broadcasters and news agencies were badly hit on Tuesday when journalists staged a 24-hour walkout in protest at government plans to scrap their 62-year-old tax privileges.

The stoppage fired a warning shot across the centre-right government's bows as civil servants, teachers, rail and power workers prepared for a 24-hour strike on Thursday against cutbacks and record unemployment.
State television channels ran short news bulletins, although the private 24-hour news broadcaster LCI offered a full service. Music dominated the France-Info radio news channel.
The strike restricted French-language services from news agencies Agence France-Presse (AFP), Associated Press and Reuters. An editor at AFP said text, graphics and picture services were disrupted.

Staff at newspaper Le Monde voted not to join the strike but many other newspapers, especially regional ones, will not appear on Wednesday in the protest over plans to scrap a 30 percent income tax deduction for professional expenses which journalists say is effectively part of their salary.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe has refused to drop a pledge to scrap tax breaks for some 100 professions including journalism. But he asked Finance Minister Jean Arthuis to ensure the measure did not put any groups at a disadvantage.
The government plans to phase out the journalists' deduction over five years along with dozens of other breaks for various professions in a reform cutting income tax for most taxpayers.

Francois Boissarie, a leader of the SNJ journalists' union, said at a demonstration outside the National Assembly that the tax break was part of their professional status, instituted to compensate for work expenses.

"If we were paranoid, we'd say the government was attacking journalists given the fact that it also plans to limit reporting of investigations. We simply note the fact that many things are happening at the same time," Boissarie said.

More than a thousand took part in the rally called by unions representing nearly 30,000 journalists as parliament began debating the 1997 budget bill. Some local unions have voted to boycott politicians who vote in favour of the government plan.
In the most extreme case, a single journalist earning 15,000 francs ($2,900) a month would end up paying 60 percent more tax after the reform than before it, government figures show.
Gaullist floor leader Michel Pericard, who had threatened to sue journalists who boycotted politicians, said on Tuesday it was time "to end an escalation for which I am partly to blame".
"Journalists need politicians, and politicians need journalists," he said.

With more than three million people out of work and tens of thousands more set to lose their jobs through public spending cuts, the strike planned for Thursday should show if the will is there for the kind of showdown which crippled the country late last year.
